name: Iatmul
confidence_why: Staalsen 1966 describes Iatmul stress as non-contrastive and predictable from the vowel (/a/ carries more intensity than /ɨ/ or /ə/), and Jendraschek 2012, known here only through a second-hand summary, likewise describes non-contrastive stress predictable from syllable shape (long vowels, then closed syllables, then the first syllable), so the two agree that stress is predictable and non-phonemic and differ only on what conditions it, while Laycock 1965 and Staalsen 1969 say nothing about Iatmul stress.
catalog_citation: Staalsen, Philip. 1966. The phonemes of Iatmul. In Frantz, C.I. et al. (eds), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 5, Pacific Linguistics A-7: 69-76. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-A7.69 (sealang.net open edition, CC BY-SA 4.0).
catalog_locator: Sec. 5 'Supra-segmental features', 5.1, p. 74 (read as image); supporting: sec. 2 vowel inventory p. 69 and 2.1.3 p. 70.
catalog_quote: 5.1. Stress, tone and length are not phonemically pertinent. Stress is sometimes related to and predictable by the vowel: /a/ is usually of greater intensity than either /ɨ/ or /ə/, Loudness is not always concurrent with highest pitch of intonation. There is no contrastive stress. 5.2. Pitch becomes important as intonation. The following intonation data is not exhaustive. [p. 74] ... The vowels of Iatmul are /ɨ/, /ə/, and /a/, forming a one dimensional system of high, mid, and low vowel. [p. 69] ... 2.1.3. Low vowel /a/ has allophones: [ʔa] not following a consonant and [a] elsewhere. This phoneme is usually of longer duration than the other vowel phonemes but there is no contrast between [a] and [aː]. [p. 70]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Staalsen (first-hand, Nyaura dialect at Brugnowi): word stress is non-contrastive and not phonemic; where predictable it follows vowel quality, the full low vowel /a/ carrying more intensity than the high/mid central vowels /ɨ, ə/; no positional (edge-based) rule is stated, and pitch functions only as intonation. The modern grammar (Jendraschek 2012: 91-93, seen only second-hand via Wikipedia) reportedly makes this a ranked weight rule: stress a long vowel, else a closed (CVC) syllable, else the word-initial syllable; diphthongs do not attract stress. Provisional reading therefore weight/quality-sensitive with an initial default (the initial default rests on the unopened Jendraschek 2012).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said by Staalsen 1966. (Laycock 1965 describes secondary stress only for Wosera Abelam, not Iatmul.)
new_statements.exceptions: Staalsen: 'sometimes'/'usually' hedges only; emphasis intonation (5.2.5) puts tone 3 on the penultimate and a 2-4 glide on the final syllable of short utterances, described as intonation not stress. Jendraschek 2012 (second-hand): in compounds the rules may apply to either the first or the second member.
new_statements.domain_note: Staalsen's statement is about the word/phonemic system generally (isolation forms from elicitation; intonation treated separately at utterance level). Laycock 1965 frames Ndu stress in terms of the 'phonological phrase' (one primary stress per pause-free stretch) but gives no Iatmul-specific rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Staalsen 1966 describes the Nyaura (upriver/western) dialect of Iatmul as spoken at Brugnowi village (his note 2: Laycock calls the Brugnowi dialect Nayura/Nyaura); Laycock 1965's outline is also Nyaura (Yamanambu). Glottolog treats Nyaura as a dialect of iatm1242 (nyau1234 if a dialect code is wanted; language-level key iatm1242 is correct). Jendraschek 2012 (not opened) is based mainly on Korogo (central Iatmul).

new_statements.quote: Iatmul phonology does not make use of tone or pitch distinctions. Although the syllables in a word are articulated with varying intensity, word stress is not an autonomous parameter, but a correlate of other factors like vowel length, syllable structure, and speed of encunciation. No example of contrastive stress has been found. [p.91] ... In polysyllabic words, stress becomes unpredictable, as differences in heaviness between syllables become less perceptible the longer the word is [...] Some general tendencies for stress assignment are, in order of decreasing importance: 1. Long vowels are stressed. 2. CVC syllables are stressed. 3. Word-initial syllables are stressed. 4. In compounds, the above rules can apply to the second member of the compound [p.92]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Staalsen 1966: stress/tone/length not phonemic, no contrastive stress, intensity tied to vowel quality) and adds the explicit weight hierarchy long vowel > closed syllable > word-initial default, the diphthong and long-/e/ exceptions, compound behaviour and secondary stress; it confirms first-hand the second-hand Wikipedia summary already held by the project (Jendraschek 2012 pp.91f, 93). Catalog classification weight-hedged / statement reading 'weight-sensitive' stands.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No tone, no contrastive stress; stress is a correlate of syllable weight and speech rate. In disyllables a syllable with a long or half-long vowel (or glottalized /aʔ/) is stressed (tiˈkaak, ˈlaavu, also affixes: yiˈvaak); when both syllables are short the first is stressed (ˈki'nya), but if the second is CVC the two are near-equal (kuli'n). Ranked tendencies: long vowel > CVC > word-initial; in longer words stress becomes unpredictable; in compounds the rules may apply to either member (assignment 'random').
new_statements.secondary_stress: When both members of a compound are polysyllabic the unstressed member takes secondary stress (avuktakwa [ˈaβukˌtaɰwɑ] 'old woman', agwataba [ˈaŋɡwɑˌtamba] 'forearm'); at slow-to-normal speed this also holds for non-compound words of four or more syllables (kwadamali [ˈkwandaˌmaɾi]); p.101 describes secondary stress as the intermediate-speech-rate residue of several intensity peaks, with fast speech leaving one peak.
new_statements.exceptions: wula'i [wuˈɾaˑʔi̯] 'to enter' and si'ba'i [sɨˈmbaˑʔi̯] 'to dislike' stressed on the 2nd syllable (glottalized vowel counts as heavy); non-glottalized diphthongs do not attract stress (wakwai [ˈwɒɡwɛi̯]); long /e/ in open syllables is not stressed (kavle [ˈkaβɾɛ], Pali'bei) except when suffix -a follows (kavle-a [kaˈβɾɛːa]); optional length shifts stress (ti'baadi' [tɨˈmbaːndɨ] ~ ti'badi' [ˈtɨmbandɨ]); subject cross-reference markers cannot be stressed after a heavy syllable or after more than one syllable (kwaami'n [ˈkwaːmɨŋ]); stress shift in guge-ak [ŋɡuˈŋɡeak].
new_statements.identity_note: Jendraschek 2012 describes Western Iatmul (self-designation Nyaula/'Nyaura'), fieldwork based in Koloku (Korogo) village on the middle Sepik; Staalsen 1966 (catalog) describes the Nyaura dialect at Brugnowi. Same dialect group.

readall_conflicts: No new source was opened, so no new disagreement can be established. The only statement actually read (Staalsen 1966, sec. 5.1, p. The second-hand Wikipedia summary of Jendraschek 2012 (pp.91f, 93) gives a different conditioning hierarchy (long vowel > CVC > word-initial; diphthongs unstressed). Both describe predictable, non-contrastive prominence, so they are compatible under 'weight-sensitive', but the conditioning factor differs (vowel quality/sonority in Staalsen vs vowel length and coda in Jendraschek) and the Jendraschek version could not be verified against the grammar. Laycock 1965 (held by the project from the earlier reading) has no Iatmul-specific stress statement.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (English), 'Iatmul language', section 'Lexical stress' (wikitext downloaded 2026-09-17), citing Jendraschek 2012 pp.91f, 93
sources.note: second-hand summary of Jendraschek 2012 pp.91f: words not distinguished by pitch or accent; stress placement rules in descending priority: (1) long vowels are stressed (ti'baadi' [tɨˈmbaːndɨ]), (2) CVC syllables are stressed (ti'kali'ka [tɨˈɡaɾɡa]), (3) otherwise word-initial syllable stressed; in compounds rules may apply to either member; diphthongs are not stressed (p.93).
